policy_title: Increase Housing Supply to 380,000 Homes Annually
stated: Increasing building of new homes to 380,000 a year across the UK, including 150,000 social homes a year, through new garden cities and community-led development of cities and towns. Allowing councils to buy land for housing based on current use value rather than on a hope-value basis by reforming the Land Compensation Act 1961.

bearing_set.reason: The policy directly targets housing supply (380,000/year including 150,000 social homes) and reforms land acquisition costs — both core drivers of affordability and social/affordable stock, the exact indicators O1 measures.

Garden cities entail large-scale greenfield development; building ~170k additional homes/year above current levels increases embodied-carbon emissions and involves land-use change that moves the emissions trajectory and water-quality indicators (construction runoff, habitat loss).

Large-scale housing supply addresses the documented constraint on UK labour mobility and productivity — workers gaining affordable access to high-opportunity areas, and reducing housing-cost drag on business investment and living standards.

150,000 social homes/year specifically targets lower-income households, while the land compensation reform (current use value vs hope value) eliminates windfall gains to landowners, both narrowing the housing-access and wealth gap between the richest and the rest.

membership_note: Four fundamentals: O1 is the direct design target; O6 captures the environmental cost of development at scale; O13 reflects the well-documented labour-mobility and productivity channel; O14 reflects the distributional design of the social housing commitment and land value reform.
